source: I look forward to watching you discover the solutions for yourself.
But I aim to not leave you entirely defenseless. I'll be here to provide assistance if you have further need of me.
How may I assist you?
Rather late for a look at the library, isn't it?
I might say the same to you.
I always seem to return to my favorite tale.
It's called 'The Great Gatsby'. Have you read it?
Afraid not. What is a Gatsby?
A tragedy from a faraway place.
Do you know what makes a tragedy excellent?
It's in the construction of the hero, you see.
One must feel such a hero is rational, relatable, and sane—doing all in their power to succeed against the odds before them.
However, there must also be some insurmountable difficulty in the hero's circumstances.
Some aspect of themself or the people around them must prevent them from achieving happiness and success. This is called the tragic flaw.
The audience feels their suffering as a form of deeply emotional release. This is called catharsis.
And no matter how rational that hero might be, they simply can't win. Not without divine intervention, at least.
I could use some of that. Divine intervention, I mean.
As I said before, my dear—my greatest desire is to nudge you along the path to enlightenment.
But make no mistake; one must be led. Not moved there posthaste.
Who... or what... are you really, Quince?
That's rather a sad tale of its own.
Good night, gentle Ophelia.
I've many a room to haunt before the evening is over, I think.
(Ah. Here's the key.)
(Apologies, Your Highness.)
(I ought to be swift.)
(Is this...)
I-it... what's this vial?
Oh, this scent!
Poison! But it cannot be—
Ophelia was... correct?
None should possess such a horrid thing.
To the flagstones. Let it sink into the earth. It shall do no harm now.
(There's nothing here.)
(Nothing at all!)
Of course Ophelia was her usual fanciful self.
What an old fool I am.
Mmm, yes. Here's the key.
Hello! Your majesty?
No response.
(I detect a faint odor. Odd.)
(Ah. This vase. What's in here?)
(A vial?)
It's hemlock. Oh, Claudius. What have you been doing?
Claudius must not have this.
I'll dump it out. There's no other way.
(I detect a faint odor... odd.)
But there's nothing here. As I thought.
Ophelia sent me on a chase. Why would she do that?
(What my husband doesn't know won't worry him.)
(I'm certain the allegations are false.)
What's that scent? Such a strange, familiar smell.
This vase...
What's this? There's something in the bottom.
A vial? W-what is—oh... Claudius.
This can't be. But it reeks of hemlock.
H-he wouldn't.
Is this-- did he use it on-- Hamlet?
No one must have this. Least of all him.
How could I have been so blind?
There's nothing here. And nothing in his desk, either.
I am a fool to have doubted him.
My husband is a good man. He must be.
But the lock is old, and weak, as I thought.
He must have something hidden here. I know it.
What's this? In the bottom, something small.
A vial.
That scent. I know that scent. Hemlock.
Oh, Claudius. You've been a rotten, vile beast, haven't you?
And now it's time to pay for your crimes. The proof is in hand. What must be done...
And his desk is mere letters, too. All of it. There's nothing here.
Y-you mean—he cannot be—innocent.
There must be something else, some... real... proof. Somewhere. Musn't there?
Hmph. Locked. Of course.
But with a twist of the hand, a knife inserted there...
I smell hemlock.
And of course. Here it is. The fool would keep it in his chambers.
This is much too potent to remain in his hands.
I'll keep it for myself. Perhaps it can be of some use to me.
But this vase is empty. There's nothing here. And nothing in these drawers, either.
I let that fool of a girl run me around. Stupid, Irma. Stupid.
Ophelia. I found it.
In his chambers, just as you described...
It was the final proof I needed. Let me not pause further. Let this proof unstick me.
And what will you do now?
Take the matter to him plainly, without further ado. You'll see.
My heart is resolved for the first time in months.
Claudius killed my father. I feel it firmly in my gut. And he'll kill again if he isn't stopped.
We cannot let that happen.
This is further proof of my Uncle's crimes. However...
It took so much for me to be sure. I no longer know what to do. And now everything's become stranger than before.
Too much is already in motion. We have no choice but to see where it leads, now.
But I will take heart in having at least stolen one of his tools.
Ophelia. I found the poison you described.
I wish that I had not.
I'm sorry, my lady. I felt you needed to see it.
Deep down, I knew.
There were whispers after Hamlet died. Of the way his body looked. The... suddenness of it.
There are no poisonous snakes in Denmark, Ophelia.
But I turned away from it all. I didn't want to know.
Even then I realized the truth. There are no good men. We women see the wickedness in their hearts. And we ignore it out of love.
I will deal with my husband. I will smite this wickedness by my own hand. I owe him that much.
I will find some immediate use of it myself, I believe.
Some rats have been troubling the kitchen for far too many years. Eighteen, to be precise.
And one of them, the Prince of them all, has scurried too far out of his hole, making trouble...
Better to be rid of him as swiftly as possible.
I shall retain it close for now, Fräulein. At the very least, the King should not have it.
That vile man. I shudder to think what pain he might have caused my lady. Or perhaps it was meant for her. I shall never know.
What will be done to the King as a result?
I've dumped it out. He shall not use it to harm again.
But Bernardo, that doesn't stop him harming others. It merely removes his tool.
There's nothing more I can do, my lady. I'm sorry. I'm merely glad Hamlet and the Queen didn't learn of it. They may have... reacted poorly.
If you ask me, this has saved us all from a bloodbath.
I went to your chambers to find you, but one of the guards let me know you'd gone to town of all places.
Despite, if memory serves, my explicit orders that you were not to be permitted to leave Elsinore.
We'll discuss that problem another day, daughter of mine.
Regardless, I was... troubled to find the vial. I still don't know what to make of it.
And what do you intend to do with it, Father?
...It is gone.
I've dumped it out upon the floor. It shall never harm further.
Father, he won't hesitate to harm others. The poison's been stopped, but not the man.
My love, no one man or woman can stop a vengeful king. It takes a proper coup.
And we are both far too small to raise one of those.
Someday, you'll understand—how futile these things can be in reality, yet feel so close to grasp in the mind's eye.
Claudius? I'm unlocking the door.
What calls you to me, love?
It's been a week or so since we had time together like this. Alone.
...Yes, you've been rather involved, haven't you.
Shall we make the beast with two backs?
I know, Claudius.
And now that chasm calls out for blood.
G-gerta, you—you know how cruel he was to me. How my father hated me. You knew!
But murder—brutal murder—that was wrong. You took my family away from me.
I am truly a fool.
I never saw it. All this time. I gave everything to Denmark, and it gave me nothing in return.
How could I have been so naïve? When Hamlet died, I thought with Claudius, things would be the same.
After all, I've known Claudius all his life. Ever since he was born. I even knew about—
Well, never mind it.
But these people see me as dispensable. Useless. Obtuse. Idiotic.
There's no longer any point to remaining here. My children and I should have left long ago.
This court has done nothing but take from us. My wife, my daughter's purity, my own dignity—I owe these people nothing more.
H-how long have you been listening?
Long enough to know that I agree.
You'd be happier away from all this. Living a simpler life.
Would you... resent me for taking you away from everything here?
Not if it meant you were happy and free.
...Oh, Ophelia.
I've been a horrid father to you, haven't I? Questioning your every move, hovering over your shoulder—
You and your brother are the only truth that matters.
Let me never forget that. Never again.
It's boarded up.
You see why I asked you, now.
Aye. But a good shove...
I heard cracking.
One more...
There. It snapped.
Is all well?
Come see for yourself.
Those are hers?
I don't think I can do this.
Everything's coming back. I feel ill.
I thought I'd forgotten her. It was easier like that.
Sometimes I merely pretended she was a dream, that she was never alive.
I have to go.
You don't have to be strong all the time, Laertes.
I know I was small. I know I don't remember her the way you do. It must be worse for you.
I don't...
I can't...
This feels wretched. I never should have come here.
Ophelia... this shack is already open.
Oh. Yes. So it is.
I... don't think I can go in there.
I'll leave yo to it.
You see why I asked you to come, now.
...And what do you expect me to do?
What men are good for. Brute force.
I heard cracking. Do that again.
It's given way a little.
I believe it's open. Perhaps.
Ophelia? Are you... all right?
Come and see this.
Are those...
I believe so. My mother's belongings.
It looks as though there's a journal, too.
Yes. My mother's belongings.
Do you... remember her?
Not at all. I have a thin memory of her face... but that could be my memory, or the portrait Father keeps on his wall.
She was very like that painting. And like you. I was old enough to remember her, a little.
I'm not... I've never been... good at things like this.
I've spent so long trying to find out anything I could about Mother. And for so long, there was nothing to find.
All of this was hidden from me.
I wish she could be here now.
Me, too.
W-well, then.
I'll leave you in peace.
I... don't understand.
This shack is already open. Is this some sort of prank?
Oh. No, no prank. I guess... I forgot? Laertes opened it earlier.
Ah. Forgot. I see.
Well, better he catch the plague than I, I suppose. Be careful in there, Ophelia.
Ugh! I can't even look at Hamlet!
